# Deepfake Detection for Images and Videos
Author: Adityaditya, B.Tech CSAI, Netaji Subhas University of Technology

*Methods, generalisation and evaluation*

A manipulated face can look convincing in one frame while its motion, pulse or lip timing gives it away over a few seconds. This computer vision project examines how researchers use those clues and asks a harder question: **does a detector still recognise a forgery when the test footage comes from somewhere new?**

*Figure 1. Three routes from a face to a prediction. The audio-visual route requires a soundtrack. Face detail from Rana et al., Figure 6, cropped from the supplied PDF ([CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)).*

> **The same detector lost 44.80 percentage points.** GLAD-ViT, trained on FaceShifter, scored 97.27% on held-out FaceShifter data and 52.47% on DFDC. Both measurements come from the published benchmark discussed in the project report.

This is a comparative literature review. It brings together two systematic reviews, examines a controlled comparison of five models and develops a proposal for testing a video detector on unseen datasets.

<!-- page -->

## What the research papers establish

**Rana et al. (2022) — What were researchers measuring?** The authors reviewed 112 papers from 2018–2020. Of the 91 studies categorised by detection method, 70 used deep learning, 16 used conventional machine learning, three used statistical tests and two used blockchain. These counts explain why CNNs dominate the review. A blockchain record answers a different question from a CNN: it can trace a file back to a registered source, while a CNN inspects the face itself.

**Ramanaharan et al. (2025) — Does performance transfer?** This review selected 108 studies and distinguished spatial, temporal, multimodal and hybrid approaches. Of those studies, 46.3% claimed their method generalised, 23.1% reported that it did not, and 30.6% did not say. The percentages count authors’ claims. A controlled transfer test is what puts a number on the size of the gap.

**Pandey et al. (2026) — What changes under a common test?** The authors compared five detectors on DFDC, Celeb-DF v2 and the Face2Face and FaceShifter subsets of FaceForensics++. They evaluated clean inputs, nine distortions and changes of dataset. Because the models shared a protocol, the results allow comparisons that pooled scores from the two reviews cannot support.

### What a detector can observe

| Evidence | How a published approach uses it |
| --- | --- |
| **Texture and boundaries** | MesoNet uses a compact CNN to learn patterns within a face crop. A spatial model can inspect a photograph or an individual video frame. |
| **Motion and physiology** | A sequence model can follow a blink across frames. FakeCatcher estimates subtle colour changes in facial regions and tests whether their pulse patterns agree. |
| **Sound and movement** | Audio-visual methods align speech with lip motion. A timing mismatch is useful evidence, though a delayed soundtrack can also occur in authentic video. |
| **Sensor traces and provenance** | Statistical approaches compare camera-noise patterns. Provenance systems instead compare the file with a trusted record, which requires a registered original. |

*Figure 2. Rana et al., Figure 6, p. 25501. The face box locates the region to analyse. The forgery decision comes later, after features have been extracted and a model has been selected. [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).*

## The benchmark in numbers

Pandey et al. trained the five models with 72 × 72 face crops and a 60/10/30 train, validation and test split. Holding the training set fixed makes one comparison especially informative.

**Read the same comparison in the original heatmap below.** In the rightmost panel, follow the bottom row (trained on FSh) to the first column (tested on DFDC). The cell reads **52.47**. Its same-dataset counterpart, **97.27**, comes from Table V of the project report. The heatmap leaves the diagonal blank because it shows transfer tests only.

*Figure 3. Project report, Figure 5, p. 6, drawn from Pandey et al., Table 5. Rows are training sets and columns are test sets. CDF = Celeb-DF v2, F2F = Face2Face, FSh = FaceShifter, DFDC = Deepfake Detection Challenge.*

| Model | Clean accuracy on FaceShifter | Mean RECAF across datasets |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| GLAD-ViT | 97.27% | 0.85 |
| EfficientNet-V2 | 94.14% | 0.82 |
| SpFreqNet | 92.33% | 0.77 |
| EfficientNet-B0 | 91.31% | 0.70 |
| MesoInception-4 | 87.27% | 0.68 |

*Source: project report, Tables V–VI, from Pandey et al. RECAF is a composite score on a 0–1 scale. Its average covers all four benchmark settings.*

Across the five models, cross-dataset accuracy ranged from **46.29% to 64.37%**. Image quality also mattered within a dataset. On DFDC, reducing illumination by 30 took SpFreqNet from **78.60% to 52.79%** accuracy. Dataset transfer and distortion therefore need separate tests.

<!-- page -->

## A detector worth testing

The evidence suggests a practical design question. If a face looks plausible in each frame, can its motion or frequency content still expose the manipulation? The project report proposes three parallel branches operating on the same tracked clip.

*Figure 4. Adapted from Figure 10 and Section VIII of the project report. The architecture is a proposal. Implementation and experimental results are future work.*

The spatial CNN would inspect local texture. The I3D and ViViT branch would follow short movements and longer relationships between frames. The frequency branch would examine spectral residuals that can reveal processing traces. Attention would learn how strongly to weight each branch for a given clip.

### How to evaluate the proposal

1. **Hold out a complete dataset.** Train on the remaining benchmarks, test on the unseen one, then rotate the held-out set. Report each result so that one easy benchmark cannot hide a weak transfer.
2. **Repeat the distortion tests.** Measure the effects of blur, noise, JPEG compression, motion blur and illumination changes. Compare training with and without corruption augmentation to determine whether it helps.
3. **Report four dimensions.** Publish clean effectiveness (E), robustness under distortion (R), cross-dataset performance (C) and compute cost (K). Cost includes parameter count, floating-point operations and per-frame latency.

**Why publish the components?** In Pandey et al.’s experiment, the entropy-based weighting assigned **3.05%** to cross-dataset performance because it varied little across the models. A model could therefore rank first overall while performing poorly on an unfamiliar dataset. The proposed evaluation gives that transfer score its own line beside the composite.

## Papers behind the project

The first three papers frame the review. The remaining eight appear in the project report’s bibliography and supply its datasets, detector designs and provenance examples.

### Core reading

1. **Rana, Nobi, Murali & Sung (2022).** The taxonomy and study counts used throughout this project. [Deepfake Detection: A Systematic Literature Review](https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2022.3154404)
2. **Ramanaharan, Guruge & Agbinya (2025).** The source for video-method families and generalisation claims. [DeepFake video detection: Insights into model generalisation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dim.2025.100099)
3. **Pandey et al. (2026).** The five-model comparison, distortion tests, cross-dataset results and RECAF scoring method. [Rethinking deepfake detection evaluation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mlwa.2026.101011)

### Supporting studies

| Paper | Contribution to the project |
| --- | --- |
| [FaceForensics++ · Rössler et al.](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICCV.2019.00009) | Establishes a benchmark of manipulated facial videos and examines how compression affects detection. |
| [DeepfakeStack · Rana & Sung](https://doi.org/10.1109/CSCloud-EdgeCom49738.2020.00021) | Shows how a second model can combine predictions from several deep detectors. |
| [MesoNet · Afchar et al.](https://doi.org/10.1109/WIFS.2018.8630761) | Introduces the compact CNN family behind the MesoInception-4 baseline. |
| [GLAD-ViT · Pandey et al.](https://doi.org/10.1080/02564602.2026.2621327) | Combines global and local attention in the transformer evaluated in the benchmark. |
| [Combating deepfake videos using blockchain and smart contracts · Hasan & Salah](https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2019.2905689) | Illustrates verification through a record of a video's origin and history. |
| [FakeCatcher · Ciftci, Demir & Yin](https://doi.org/10.1109/TPAMI.2020.3009287) | Uses biological signals in portrait videos as evidence of authenticity. |
| [LW-DeepFakeNet · Masud et al.](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11760-023-02633-9) | Provides a lightweight CNN–LSTM design relevant to the question of inference cost. |
| [Hierarchical supervisions with two-stream network · Liang et al.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patrec.2023.05.029) | Provides a two-stream detection example behind the report’s discussion of spatial and frequency evidence. |

**Project materials.** The supplied project report is the source for the benchmark figures and proposed architecture. The methods handout organises the detector families, and the presentation script motivates the focus on generalisation. The ZIP includes the supplied Rana et al. paper and the methods handout for offline reading.
